curator.photoShows: No source photo shows a standing march with arm swing. Closest frames: Moving Claw Series (a walk, then a high-knee claw running drill); Step-up with Knee Raise (stepping onto a box and driving the knee, hands held at the chest); Walking, Treadmill (walking on a treadmill).
curator.why: The source has no march exercise. Moving Claw Series is a pawing sprint-form drill: frame 0 is a head-down walk and frame 1 is a claw/high-knee position, not a rhythmic march. Step-up with Knee Raise has a step and no arm swing. Walking, Treadmill uses a machine. Each one differs in action or equipment.

curator.photoShows: Gym turf, side view. Frame 0: relaxed upright stance with one foot slightly forward and arms bent. Frame 1: a low skip. The feet are close together near the ground, one foot is touching down while the other lifts only slightly, the arms swing opposite to the legs, and the torso is upright.
curator.why: The source instructions describe a step-hop skip done 'maintaining close contact with the ground and reduce air time', which is a low-amplitude skip. Position (standing, travelling), equipment (none), action (skip, not a run or a high-knee A-skip) and body part (feet and calves) all match the drill. The only difference is tempo ('fast' versus easy), and a still photo cannot show tempo. The pattern and amplitude are the same.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The set-up matches: standing, travelling forward on turf, no equipment or support. Frame 1 shows a skip kept close to the ground. The front foot is planted under the body, the rear leg lifts only a few inches with a bent knee, there is no high knee drive and no visible flight, the arms swing opposite the legs and the torso stays upright. That is the low-amplitude version, not a power or A-skip with big knee drive. The source's own instructions say to 'maintain close contact with the ground and reduce air time', which fits the cue to stay light and keep contacts quiet. The source is 'fast' and the drill is easy, but that is a tempo difference, not a different position or pattern. One caveat: the still frames cannot show forefoot contact (the planted foot looks fairly flat) and could be read as a short jog stride. With the drill name and cue alongside, someone copying them would still perform a low skip.

I viewed both frames. The athlete is standing on open turf with no equipment, and he moves forward between the frames, so it is a travelling drill as the 2 x 15 m dose needs. Frame 1 shows a low skip contact. The support foot lands on the forefoot with the heel just off the turf. The other foot only clears the ground slightly behind, with a soft bent knee. The arms swing opposite the legs and the trunk stays upright. There is no high knee drive, no bound and no visible flight. The source's own instruction is a step-hop skip 'maintaining close contact with the ground and reduce air time', which is exactly a low-amplitude skip. Copying these frames gives a quiet, forefoot-light low skip, not a high skip, A-skip, bound or march. The word 'fast' in the source is about tempo, which a still frame cannot show; the pattern and amplitude match the cue. The one limit is that a still image cannot show the hop, so frame 1 alone could pass for a jog stride. That is inherent to stills and does not contradict the drill.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows a lateral shuffle with an arm reach. Closest frames: Side to Side Box Shuffle (feet alternating on top of a box); Lateral Cone Hops (two-foot hops over cones); Monster Walk (band around the ankles, hands on hips).
curator.why: Side to Side Box Shuffle needs a box and is a crossover jump onto it. Lateral Cone Hops are two-footed hops over cones. Monster Walk is a slow banded walk with no shuffle and no reach. None of them shows a free athletic-stance shuffle with a reach. The equipment and the action both differ.

curator.photoShows: Carioca Quick Step, front view on indoor turf. Frame 0: standing tall with feet a few inches apart and one arm raised. Frame 1: the right leg kicked back and flexed behind the body on its own side, the left leg planted, and the arms pumping. No crossover of the feet and no pelvic rotation is visible.
curator.why: The app drill is a classic carioca: lateral travel with the trailing leg crossing alternately in front and behind, and the pelvis rotating while the chest stays tall. The source 'Carioca Quick Step' is a different quick-feet drill: step behind, then pull the knee straight up, and explicitly 'avoid turning your feet'. Its frames show no crossover step and no hip rotation, so they would not teach the hip-switch action. This is a near miss with a similar name, not a match.

curator.photoShows: No source exercise shows a backpedal or a backward run finishing in a march. The only backward-travel item is Sled Overhead Backward Walk, which uses a sled and is not viewed as plausible. Gait photos viewed (Moving Claw Series, Fast Skipping, Trail Running/Walking) all travel forward.
curator.why: No backpedal exists in the source. A forward run, skip or march photo would show the wrong direction and the wrong action. Sled walks add equipment.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows small, stiff-ankle, in-place bounces with no equipment. Closest: Rope Jumping (bouncing on the forefoot while turning a jump rope); Lateral Cone Hops (larger tucked hops travelling over cones).
curator.why: Rope Jumping has the right small forefoot bounce but adds a jump rope, and the equipment must match. Cone or hurdle hops are bigger travelling hops over obstacles, not a pogo pulse. The source has no unloaded, equipment-free ankle pogo.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows an A-skip (thigh driven to about hip height with a dorsiflexed foot during a skip). Fast Skipping frame 1 shows a low skip with minimal knee lift. Moving Claw Series frame 1 shows a high knee, but frame 0 is a walk and the drill is a pawing claw run. Linear Acceleration Wall Drill shows a knee drive while leaning against a wall.
curator.why: The A-skip's defining feature is the high knee drive inside a skip rhythm. Fast Skipping is deliberately low-amplitude with no knee drive. Moving Claw Series is a different sprint-form drill (heel to glute, then claw down) and its pair is a walk plus a knee position. The wall drill is a supported lean (different support and position). Each is a different drill for the same region.

curator.photoShows: Trail Running/Walking: a runner on an outdoor dirt trail, front view then side view, two different scenes. Running, Treadmill: running on a treadmill, seen from behind and from the side. Single-Cone Sprint Drill: quick foot chops around a cone.
curator.why: No source photo shows a straight-line acceleration run on flat ground. The treadmill run uses a machine (wrong support). The trail run is endurance trail running or hiking on uneven terrain, shot as two unrelated scenes, not a rehearsal stride. The cone drill is a circling footwork drill. These are similar-looking photos of other activities, so the result is none.

curator.photoShows: No source shows it. The closest, Kneeling_Hip_Flexor, shows a long half-kneeling lunge with the back knee on a pad, hands on hips, the front shin about vertical and a small forward weight shift for a hip flexor stretch.
curator.why: The drill is a short half-kneeling stance with the front knee driven well past the toes and the front heel kept down, which loads the front ankle and soleus. Kneeling_Hip_Flexor is a different drill for a different region: a long stance with the front shin near vertical, so the photo never shows ankle dorsiflexion range. Standing_Soleus_And_Achilles_Stretch is standing in a split stance, not half-kneeling, and it is a static stretch for the back leg. The source has no half-kneeling ankle mobilization.

curator.photoShows: Wall candidates show a straight back leg calf stretch with the hands on the wall (Calf_Stretch_Hands_Against_Wall) and a lean with both feet back and the forearms on the wall (Calf_Stretch_Elbows_Against_Wall). Standing_Soleus_And_Achilles_Stretch shows a split stance with both knees bent and no wall.
curator.why: The drill puts the front foot a few inches from a wall and drives the front knee forward to touch the wall with the heel down, which tests the front ankle. None of the candidates shows this. The wall stretches lengthen the back leg's gastrocnemius with a straight knee, far from the wall. The soleus stretch has no wall and works the back leg. All are static calf stretches of a different leg, position and action, so using one would teach the wrong movement.

curator.photoShows: A close-up of the lower legs and feet, standing with no equipment. The left foot stays planted while the right foot is lifted a couple of inches off the floor and circles at the ankle. In frame 0 the toes point up with the sole showing (dorsiflexed). In frame 1 the toes point down and across (plantarflexed). The shin stays still, so the motion comes from the ankle.
curator.why: Same drill. The body position matches: standing on one leg with the other foot free. No equipment is needed; the source suggests holding a rack, but none shows in the cropped photo. The action is a circle drawn with the foot, and the moving part is the ankle. The source instructions describe single-leg ankle circles: lift one foot about 2 inches and draw a circle with the big toe. The frames show the circle coming from the ankle, which fits the cue about not twisting the knee.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. They are a close-up from the shins down. The person stands on the floor with no visible equipment, and one foot (the subject's right) is lifted a couple of inches. The other foot stays flat. Frame 0 shows the lifted foot dorsiflexed, toes up with the sole facing the camera. Frame 1 shows it plantarflexed and turned in, toes pointing down and across. Those are opposite points of a circle, not a straight up-and-down ankle pump. The lifted shin stays vertical and in the same place in both frames, so the motion comes from the ankle, which is what the cue 'Move from the ankle rather than twisting the knee' asks for. The position (standing, single leg), the support (none needed), the body part (ankle), the action (circling, not holding) and the laterality (one leg at a time) all match a standing single-leg ankle circle. The source text says to hold a squat rack for balance, but the close-up doesn't show the hands. The drill doesn't require hand support or forbid it, so nothing in the frames conflicts with the drill. Someone copying these frames would do the named drill correctly.

I looked at both frames. It's a close-up of the lower legs, standing, with no equipment in shot. The left foot (image right) stays planted. The right foot (image left) is lifted a couple of inches off the floor. In frame 0 the ankle is dorsiflexed, with the toes up and the sole toward the camera. In frame 1 the ankle is plantarflexed and the foot has swung down and medially. The shin stays close to vertical and the knee shows no visible twist, so the motion comes from the ankle, as the cue asks. The two frames are roughly opposite points of one ankle circle, not a single flex-point line. The name 'circles' and the 'each direction' dose make the circular path clear. Copying it gives the named drill: single-leg, standing, ankle-only circles. The source also suggests holding a rack for balance. That support is out of frame and the drill doesn't forbid it, so it doesn't conflict. Minor caveat: two stills can't show the full circle, so the cue or name has to carry it. The photos themselves don't contradict it.

curator.photoShows: Only general locomotion photos exist. Trail_Running_Walking shows a man running on a dirt trail. Walking_Treadmill is a cardio machine. No source shows a slow walk that deliberately rolls from heel to toe.
curator.why: The drill is a controlled walk that rolls from heel strike to toe-off to work the tibialis and calves. Trail_Running_Walking shows running, which is a different action. A treadmill walk is a machine cardio exercise, not this drill. The source has no heel-walk, toe-walk or heel-to-toe drill.

curator.photoShows: The only toe-raise sources are loaded and machine-based. Rocking_Standing_Calf_Raise has a barbell on the back in a rack and rocks between heels and toes. Smith_Machine_Reverse_Calf_Raises has a Smith bar on the back with the heels on a platform.
curator.why: The drill is done standing with the back against a wall and the feet in front, lifting the toes with body weight and the wall as support. Both candidates use a barbell or Smith bar and no wall. Rocking_Standing_Calf_Raise also alternates calf raises with toe raises, and its frames mostly show heel raises. Implement, support and action all differ. No source shows a bodyweight wall-supported toe raise.

curator.photoShows: Every calf raise source is stationary: dumbbells on a board (Standing_Dumbbell_Calf_Raise), a barbell in a rack (Rocking_Standing_Calf_Raise), a Smith machine, a calf machine or bands. No source shows walking on the balls of the feet.
curator.why: The drill is walking on the toes with heels high for slow steps, so it is a locomotion action. The candidates are calf raises done in place, mostly with external load, which breaks the rule that a walk is not a stationary move. No source shows a toe walk or calf-raise walk.

curator.photoShows: Frame 0: athlete on all fours (hands under shoulders, both knees on the floor, neutral back). Frame 1: same quadruped base with one bent knee lifted and swung out and back, partway through the circle.
curator.why: Same position (quadruped), no equipment, same action (the bent knee draws a circle at the hip) and same moving part (the femur at the hip). The source's instructions describe exactly this: from hands and knees, lift one bent knee and rotate the femur in a big circle, then switch sides. The back stays flat in both frames, which fits the cue. Standing_Hip_Circles is the standing version and was rejected because the position differs.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames, and the set-up matches the drill. Frame 0 shows a quadruped on the floor with no equipment: hands under shoulders, both knees down, neutral spine. Frame 1 keeps the same base while one bent knee is lifted out to the side and slightly back, part-way around the arc. Body position (all fours), support (bare floor), the part moving (femur, with the knee as the pointer), laterality (one side at a time) and range all fit 'Quadruped hip circle'. The trunk and hands stay planted and the low back stays fairly neutral, which matches the cue to keep the low back quiet. This is not the standing version (Standing_Hip_Circles), not a held stretch, and not a different hip drill. Two still frames cannot show the full circle, so frame 1 could be read alone as a fire-hydrant abduction. The item's name and the source's own instructions ('rotate the femur in an arc ... big circle with your knee') settle that, so the photo would not teach the wrong movement.

I viewed both frames. This source is the quadruped hip circle itself. Its own instructions say to get on hands and knees, lift one bent knee and move the femur in a big arc, then switch sides. Frame 0 shows the all-fours base: hands on the floor under the shoulders, both knees down, flat back. In frame 1 the base is the same, the near knee stays bent and is lifted off the floor and out to the side into abduction, and the trunk and pelvis stay level. That is one point on the circle. The two frames match the drill on every point: same position (quadruped), no equipment, same body part (femur moving at the hip) and one side at a time. The only thing to watch is that a still frame can't show a circle. Copying frame 1 alone could look like a fire-hydrant lift. With the name and the 'femur explores the range' cue, though, the photo leads to the circle with a quiet low back, not to a similar but different drill. It is not the standing version (Standing_Hip_Circles), which is a separate drill.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a single-leg hinge with the pelvis rotating open and closed over the stance hip while holding a support.
curator.why: The source has no hip airplane. Closest candidates: Kettlebell_One-Legged_Deadlift is a single-leg hinge holding a kettlebell, with no support and no pelvic rotation, so the equipment and action differ. Standing_Hip_Circles is upright on one leg, circling a raised knee, which is a different drill. Name, keyword ('airplane', 'rotate') and instruction-text searches found nothing else.

curator.photoShows: The only '90/90' source (90_90_Hamstring) shows the athlete lying supine, holding one thigh at 90 degrees and straightening that knee toward the ceiling.
curator.why: 90_90_Hamstring is a supine active hamstring stretch, not a seated 90/90 hip switch. Position (supine vs seated), action (knee extension vs windshield-wiper hip rotation) and target all differ. Seated alternatives (Seated_Glute, Groin_and_Back_Stretch, Seated_Floor_Hamstring_Stretch) are partner, butterfly or hamstring stretches with no 90/90 leg position or switching.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a shin-box (90/90) sit rising through the knees to kneeling or standing.
curator.why: No shin-box or get-up-from-90/90 exercise exists in the source. 'Shin', 'box' and 'get-up' only return Turkish get-ups (kettlebell overhead, a different pattern) and box jumps or box squats. 90_90_Hamstring is supine and unrelated.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a wide-knee quadruped/frog position rocking the hips back and forth.
curator.why: Every adductor or groin source is a different position or action. Groin_and_Back_Stretch is seated with soles together, curling the trunk down. Adductor_Groin is supine with a partner holding the legs apart. Lying_Bent_Leg_Groin is a supine partner butterfly. Hip_Circles_prone is quadruped but knees narrow, circling one knee. Frog_Hops is a jumping drill. None shows the frog position with a rock back.

curator.photoShows: No source shows half-kneeling with the free leg straight out to the side and the hips shifting back.
curator.why: Kneeling_Hip_Flexor is half-kneeling but in a sagittal lunge (front foot forward, back knee down), shifting the hips forward into a hip-flexor stretch. The leg position and direction of movement differ, and neither frame shows a lateral leg or a rock-back. Intermediate_Groin_Stretch is supine with a band. Seated_Floor_Hamstring_Stretch is seated. None matches.

curator.photoShows: The closest source (Barbell_Side_Split_Squat) shows a wide stance under a loaded back-squat barbell, sinking toward one bent leg while the other leg stays nearly straight.
curator.why: Barbell_Side_Split_Squat has the same lateral side-to-side squat pattern, but the athlete carries a barbell on his back, while the Cossack shift is unloaded bodyweight mobility. The equipment mismatch disqualifies it under the rules. No bodyweight lateral or Cossack squat exists in the source; 'cossack' returns 0 hits, and Plie_Dumbbell_Squat and Sit_Squats are bilateral squats.

curator.photoShows: Frame 0: standing tall, side view, feet staggered (one foot slightly ahead), no equipment, hands at sides. Frame 1: long standing split stance, rear heel up, both knees bent, rear hip in extension (rear thigh behind the trunk line), trunk near-upright with a slight forward lean and head down, hands by the thighs. Bodyweight, on a mat.
curator.why: Same position (standing split stance, not kneeling), same equipment (none), same region (rear-leg hip flexors). The source's own instruction is the drill's action: 'bend both knees and lift the back heel off the floor as you press the hip forward', so the pair shows the drill's start and its end range. The drill's tags have no overhead component (unlike half-kneel-reach), so 'reach tall' reads as a posture cue and nothing defining is missing. Caveats a verifier should weigh: frame 0's stagger is shorter than frame 1's stance, so the pair can read slightly like stepping into a lunge; frame 1 shows a deeper range than a small pulse; the trunk leans a little forward. Downgrade to none if 'tall, tucked trunk' is treated as defining. The other candidates fail on position: Kneeling_Hip_Flexor (half-kneeling), Worlds_Greatest_Stretch (frame 1 is an elbow drop), Crossover_Reverse_Lunge (rotation), Split_Squats (jumping switch).

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. They don't show a pulse done in a fixed split stance. In frame 0 he stands tall with only a short stagger: the rear foot sits about 59% of the way along the mat, roughly a foot-length behind the front foot. That is not a split stance. In frame 1 the rear foot has stepped back to about 89% of the mat while the front foot stays near 25-29%, so the stance roughly doubles in length. He has also sunk into a deep lunge: front thigh near parallel, rear knee bent hard and only a few inches off the mat, trunk tipped slightly forward with the chin down. Someone copying these two frames would step back and drop into the bottom of a reverse lunge or split squat. The drill keeps the feet planted in a long split stance and makes small rhythmic forward presses of the pelvis while the trunk stays tall. Both the stance set-up and the range differ (stationary drill shown as a step-and-sink), and the head-down forward lean works against the 'reach tall' cue. A different, deep-lunge stretch photo is not this drill.

The two frames do not show a pulse inside a fixed split stance. They show the athlete stepping from a short stance into a deep lunge. In frame 0 he stands tall in a short stagger, rear heel flat, feet about 0.3 of the mat length apart. In frame 1 the rear foot has moved far back: the gap is about 0.6 of the mat length, scaled against the mat. The rear heel is up, the front knee is bent to about 90 degrees and the rear knee hovers just above the mat. So the movement between frames is a step back and a drop into a low lunge, which is a reverse lunge or deep lunge stretch, not small rhythmic hip-forward pulses from a set split stance. Frame 1 also goes against the cue: the trunk leans forward and the head is down, with no tall posture or reach (the arms hang by the thighs), and no pelvic tuck is visible. Copying these frames would teach a lunge, not a split-stance hip flexor pulse. Frame 1 also goes well beyond the source's own instructions ('left foot slightly in front', 'can't get a thorough, deep stretch in this position').

curator.photoShows: Closest is Kneeling_Hip_Flexor: half-kneeling on a pad, hands on hips, the same forward-shifted hold in both frames, with no arm movement.
curator.why: The drill's defining feature is the arm reaching overhead (cue: 'as the arm reaches overhead'; regions include lats). Kneeling_Hip_Flexor has the right half-kneeling position, but both frames show a hands-on-hips static hold with no overhead reach, which the rules exclude. Worlds_Greatest_Stretch is a lunge with the rear knee off the floor and an elbow drop. Standing_Hip_Flexors is standing. Intermediate_Hip_Flexor_and_Quad_Stretch is a prone belt stretch. The overhead stretches in the source (Overhead_Stretch, Upward_Stretch, Standing_Lateral_Stretch) are not half-kneeling. No source shows half-kneeling with an overhead reach.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Runners_Stretch. Frame 0: standing tall, side view. Frame 1: stationary staggered stance, front heel down with toes up, back knee slightly bent, trunk folded with a clearly rounded back, both hands clasping the front ankle and held there.
curator.why: The drill is a walking, dynamic sweep: step out, hinge from the hips, sweep the hands past the front foot, rise and step forward. Runners_Stretch frame 1 has a similar foot set-up but shows a static hold gripping the ankle with a rounded spine rather than a hip hinge. That would teach holding and rounding, not a walking sweep. Its source text also describes a different, hands-on-floor runner's lunge. Standing_Toe_Touches is a two-foot static forward fold. Standing_Hamstring_and_Calf_Stretch is a static strap stretch. Inchworm walks the hands out to a plank. Front_Leg_Raises is a leg swing. None shows the walking sweep.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Kettlebell_One-Legged_Deadlift. Frame 0: standing, walking toward camera, kettlebell in one hand. Frame 1: single-leg hinge placing the kettlebell on the floor, rear leg lifted with the knee clearly bent, and the pelvis and trunk rotated open.
curator.why: The drill is an unloaded single-leg RDL reach. The only single-leg RDL in the source has a kettlebell in hand, and equipment must match (none vs kettlebell). Frame 1 also contradicts the cue: the rear leg is bent instead of reaching long through the heel, and the hips are rotated open instead of square. No bodyweight single-leg hinge exists in the source (searched one-leg, single leg, deadlift, hinge, balance). Leg_Lift is a supported standing leg curl, a different action.

curator.photoShows: Single_Leg_Glute_Bridge: supine, one leg held straight up throughout; frame 0 has the hips on the floor, frame 1 has them raised. Butt_Lift_Bridge and Pelvic_Tilt_Into_Bridge: two-foot bridge from the floor to hips up.
curator.why: A bridge march holds the hips up on both feet while alternately lifting one bent knee, keeping the pelvis level. Single_Leg_Glute_Bridge raises and lowers the hips with a straight leg held in the air, so the action differs: hips move and legs do not alternate. Butt_Lift_Bridge and Pelvic_Tilt_Into_Bridge are plain two-foot bridges, the base movement without the march, which the rules forbid proposing. The word 'march' appears nowhere in the source.

curator.photoShows: Front view, mini-band around both ankles, hands on hips, toes pointing forward in both frames. Frame 0: wide lateral stance in a slight quarter-squat with the band stretched. Frame 1: trailing foot brought in to a narrow stance (band still taut). The body has shifted sideways toward image-right, and its distance from the camera is essentially unchanged.
curator.why: Standing, mini-band at the ankles, toes forward, side-step out then trailing foot in: these are the two positions of a band lateral walk, and abductors are the primary muscle. The source text describes forward steps, but the frames show a lateral step. The torso moves about 30 px sideways between frames, the feet stay at the same depth, and there is no size or perspective change that forward walking would produce. So the photos depict the lateral walk, not a forward monster walk. Caveats: frame 1's feet come closer together than ideal for even band tension, and the source text disagrees with the photos. Band_Hip_Adductions is an anchored-band adduction, not a walk.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames and the raw images. Front view, standing, a mini-band looped around both ankles (no knee band visible), hands on hips, toes pointing essentially forward. Frame 0 shows a wide stance with slightly bent knees and a taut band. In frame 1 the image-left foot has come in to a narrow stance and the band is still taut. After allowing for the camera's roughly 25 px pan (seen in the wall-panel seams), the image-right foot stays put, the image-left foot moves in about 100 px, and the body shifts sideways. Head size and floor line barely change, so this is a lateral step pattern, not the forward monster walk the source's text describes. Copying it gives a band lateral walk: same position, same equipment and support, same action, same body part. One small set-up difference: frame 1 is more upright, with knees nearly straight, where coaches usually hold a quarter squat. That doesn't make it a different drill or break the cue (toes forward, band tension kept).

Despite the source's name and text (a forward/backward monster walk), the photos show a lateral band walk. Front view; a mini-band sits around the ankles in both frames; hands on hips; toes point forward (a slight natural turn-out at most). Camera depth is unchanged: the floor line and the feet sit at the same height in the image, so there is no forward walking. Between frames the image-left foot moves about 80 px toward the other foot, which stays nearly in place (about 15 px of shift). The body's centre moves about 50 px sideways. That is a side-step with the trailing foot following, and the band stays taut in the narrow stance. Copying the frames gives a band lateral walk with even tension and toes forward. Minor note: frame 1 is more upright than frame 0's quarter-squat, so a coach may want to cue staying low between steps. It does not change the drill.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a bodyweight reverse lunge that finishes with a knee drive. Crossover_Reverse_Lunge: both frames show the bottom of a bodyweight rear lunge, the second with the torso rotated across the front leg, and there is no knee drive. Dumbbell_Rear_Lunge: standing with dumbbells, then a rear-lunge bottom. Step-up_with_Knee_Raise: a box step-up, then a standing knee raise.
curator.why: The drill is a bodyweight reverse lunge followed by driving the rear knee up to a single-leg balance. Crossover_Reverse_Lunge has the right lunge and no equipment, but its action is a torso rotation at the bottom and it has no knee-drive frame. Dumbbell_Rear_Lunge adds dumbbells and has no knee drive. Step-up_with_Knee_Raise has the knee drive, but out of a box step-up rather than a reverse lunge. Searches for lunge, knee, drive and step found nothing else.

curator.photoShows: Goblet_Squat (kettlebell): standing holding a kettlebell at the chest, then a deep squat with the elbows inside the knees. Bodyweight_Squat: hands behind the head, standing, then a parallel squat with no pry. Sit_Squats: arms out in front, partial squat. Groin_and_Back_Stretch: seated butterfly, curling the elbows down to the thighs.
curator.why: The drill is a deep bodyweight squat in which the elbows pry the knees apart. Only Goblet_Squat shows the pry (its instructions say to use the elbows to push the knees out at the bottom), but it holds a kettlebell, and the drill is named bodyweight, so the equipment does not match. Bodyweight_Squat and Sit_Squats are bodyweight but show no elbow pry: the hands are behind the head or held out in front. Groin_and_Back_Stretch is seated. No source shows an unloaded deep squat pry.

curator.photoShows: Frame 0: standing tall, feet shoulder width, hands behind the head, no equipment. Frame 1: the bottom of a bodyweight squat, thighs about parallel, knees tracking over the toes, whole foot flat, chest up.
curator.why: Both are a standing bodyweight squat: same position, no equipment, same squat pattern and range, with the whole foot on the floor as the cue asks. The three-second lowering is a speed prescription that no photo can show, and it changes neither the position nor the movement. Sit_Squats was rejected: it is a partial squat above parallel, reversed quickly, with the arms out in front, so it does not show a full squat.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The position and set-up match: standing, feet about shoulder width, no equipment, hands behind the head. Frame 1 is the bottom of a bodyweight squat, thighs about parallel, knees over the toes, both heels and the whole foot flat, chest up. That is the cue's 'whole foot connected'. The three-second descent is a timing instruction a photo cannot show, and nothing in the frames contradicts it. The hands-behind-head arm position comes from the source's own instructions and does not change the squat pattern. Someone copying these frames would do a bodyweight squat to parallel, so the tempo version is fully represented.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0 shows him standing tall, feet about shoulder width, hands behind the head, no equipment. Frame 1 shows the same man at the bottom of a bodyweight squat: thighs about parallel, knees out over the toes, heels and whole foot flat, chest up, hands still behind the head. Between the frames the hips and knees bend in a single squat down and back up. Nothing else changes: no implement, no shift in stance, no stepping. Copying these frames gives a bodyweight squat to about parallel with the whole foot down, which is the drill. A photo cannot show the three-second tempo, but the pattern, stance, implement (none) and depth all match. Holding the hands behind the head is a normal coaching choice and does not alter the movement.

curator.photoShows: Barbell_Side_Split_Squat: wide stance with a barbell across the back, then a side lunge bending one knee and hip. Groin_and_Back_Stretch: seated groin stretch. No bodyweight lateral lunge exists in the source.
