The only lateral-lunge photo, Barbell_Side_Split_Squat, carries a back-loaded barbell, so the equipment does not match. Searches for lateral, side, shift, wide stance, groin and adductor found only seated or lying groin stretches, foam rolling, band and machine adduction, and lateral jumps. None is a standing bodyweight side lunge.

curator.photoShows: Frame 0: deep forward lunge on a mat, no equipment. The front foot is flat, the back knee is just above the floor, the torso is upright and the hands hang by the front thigh. Frame 1: a long lunge with the back leg straight. The near hand is planted on the floor and the other arm is bent, so the elbow drops down inside the front foot: the elbow-drop position.
curator.why: This is the same named drill: a bodyweight lunge, then the elbow dropped to the inside of the front foot. Position, support (none, on the floor) and the first two movements match the cue 'lunge, elbow drop, and rotation'. Caveat: neither frame shows the thoracic rotation. The source's own third stage is a front-leg hamstring stretch, not a rotation, so the photos cover two of the drill's three positions. They show nothing wrong. A verifier who requires the rotation to be pictured should overrule this to none.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. Frame 0 is an upright deep lunge on a mat: back knee just above the floor, torso vertical, hands hanging. Frame 1 is a long lunge with the back leg straight, the near hand planted inside the front foot and the far elbow dropped low beside the front foot. That covers the lunge and the elbow drop, but the third part named in the cue, the rotation (open the chest and reach the arm to the ceiling), is in neither frame. The rotation is what makes this a thoracic spine drill (regions: hips, thoracic spine), just as the brief says a drill whose defining overhead reach is missing does not match. The source is also a different variant: its instructions are three static holds of 10–20 s each (upright lunge, elbow down, then hands either side of the foot with the front leg straightened for a hamstring stretch), with no rotation at all. Someone copying these frames would do lunge to elbow drop and hold it, leaving out the rotation the cue asks for.

I viewed both frames and enlarged the arms in frame 1. Frame 0 is a static upright lunge: torso vertical, back knee just above the mat, hands hanging by the front thigh. Frame 1 is a long lunge with the back leg straight and one hand planted on the mat. The other arm is bent with its fist hovering beside the front shin, and the elbow hangs above the front foot; it does not reach the floor. The only action shown is folding from an upright lunge down to a hand-down, partial elbow-drop position. Neither frame shows a rotation: no arm reaching up toward the ceiling and no turned chest. Yet the cue names three parts (lunge, elbow drop, rotation), and the thoracic spine region depends only on the rotation. The source confirms this: it is a static three-part hold whose third part straightens the front leg for a hamstring stretch, with no rotation at all. Copying these frames gives a lunge with an elbow drop (a Spiderman-lunge cousin) that leaves out the drill's defining rotation. That is the same situation as a reach drill whose defining overhead reach is missing.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a snap-down: a fast drop from a tall, arms-overhead stance into an athletic stance that is then held. The landing sources all involve jumping, either jumps with a landing (Rocket_Jump, Star_Jump, Knee_Tuck_Jump, Bench_Jump, Frog_Hops) or drops from a box (Linear_Depth_Jump, Depth_Jump_Leap).
curator.why: A snap-down has no jump and no box: the athlete pulls the arms down sharply and drops in place into a quarter squat, then holds it. Searches for snap, land, stick, absorb, athletic and drop down found only jump drills, whose action is a take-off, and depth jumps, which start from a box. Showing a jump or a depth drop for this drill would teach the wrong movement.

curator.photoShows: Front view, no load. He holds a small black object at the chest that is not part of the exercise. Frame 0: one foot planted forward on the step and the knee bent, with the other leg behind: the start of the step-up. Frame 1: standing tall on one leg with the other knee driven high, balancing at the top. The box is barely visible, only as a grey edge at the bottom of frame 0.
curator.why: The source's instructions are this drill: bodyweight step-up onto a box, extend through the front leg, drive the other knee as high as possible, step down, alternate. Position, the support (a box), the action (step-up into a knee drive, balanced at the top) and the leg moving all match. Confidence is medium for two reasons. The box is almost out of frame, so its height (the drill says 'low') cannot be confirmed. And he holds an incidental small object. Neither changes the movement shown.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames and enlarged the lower part of each. Set-up: front view, body weight only, a box in front of him. In frame 0 the box's near top edge shows as a grey strip at the very bottom. The non-tattooed front foot is in full view on top of that edge, while the tattooed trail leg's foot drops below it and out of sight, which means the front foot is on the box and the trail foot is on the floor. So this is the step-up with the drive foot planted, not a floor lunge. Frame 1: same laterality (standing on the non-tattooed leg), standing tall with the tattooed knee driven to chest height, balancing at the top. That matches 'balance briefly at the top'. From the knee bend in frame 0 the step looks low to moderate, about 20–35 cm, which is consistent with a low step-up. Caveats: the box is barely visible, and he holds a small black object at his chest that is not part of the drill. Neither changes the movement someone would copy.

I viewed both frames and enlarged the bottom of each. Frame 0, front view: his right foot is planted forward on a grey step surface whose edge is visible right under the shoe, with the front knee only slightly bent, so the step is low. The tattooed left leg is behind and its foot drops below the frame edge. That foot is farther from the camera yet sits lower in the image than the front foot, so the front foot must be raised on the step. Frame 1: he stands tall on the right leg with the tattooed left knee driven to about hip height, balancing on one leg. Laterality is consistent: the leg on the step becomes the stance leg, and the trailing leg is the one driven up. Between the frames the action is to push through the planted foot, stand up onto the step, drive the trailing knee and balance at the top. That is exactly the drill and its cue. He holds a small black object at the chest, which is incidental and not a load, and the stance foot is out of frame in frame 1. Neither changes the movement someone would copy.

curator.photoShows: Man on hands and knees on a mat. Frame 0: flat, neutral back with the head level. Frame 1: spine fully rounded (flexed), belly drawn in, head dropped.
curator.why: Same position (quadruped), no equipment, and the same spine moving in the same plane. The frames go from neutral into segmental flexion, the 'cat' half of the cat-camel. Caveat: the extension (arched) half is not pictured. The source's text says to hold the rounded position for 15 s, but the two frames read as neutral-to-flexion movement. The photo is incomplete rather than wrong: it teaches the right setup and direction, and no other source entry shows quadruped spinal flexion/extension. Rear_Leg_Raises shares the same frame 0 but its frame 1 is a leg extension, so it is not a cat-camel.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The set-up matches: he is on hands and knees on a mat with no equipment. The range does not. Frame 0 is a neutral, flat back with the head hanging down, and frame 1 is a full round (spine flexion). Neither frame shows the extension half, where the back sags and the chest and head lift. A cat-camel is defined by moving between flexion and extension, so someone copying these frames would only go from neutral to rounded, which is half the drill. The source is also a 15-second end-range flexion hold ('Hold for 15 seconds'). The drill's cue says the opposite: 'this is not a loaded end-range drill.' This is a static stretch for the same region, not the segmental flexion-extension drill. No other source in the library shows the extension (camel/cow) position either.

I viewed both frames. The man stays on all fours, and the only movement is from a flat back (frame 0) to a fully rounded back with the head dropped (frame 1). Cat-camel moves the spine back and forth between rounding and arching, segment by segment. These frames never show the arching half: no sagging lumbar spine and no lifted chest or head. The source's own instructions are to round and hold for 15 seconds, which makes it a static cat stretch, not the cat-camel cycle. Someone copying these frames would repeat neutral-to-rounded (or hold the rounded position) and miss the extension half of the drill. The position and equipment match, but the action does not. There is no other cat-cow or camel source in the 876-entry list.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a quadruped thoracic rotation (one hand planted, the other arm or elbow rotating up toward the ceiling).
curator.why: Every quadruped source entry shows a different action. Cat_Stretch is spinal flexion. Rear_Leg_Raises is a straight-leg extension. Glute_Kickback is a bent-knee hip extension. Hip_Circles_prone is a knee circle. Chest_Stretch_on_Stability_Ball has the elbow on a ball with the torso sinking, a pec stretch with no rotation. Childs_Pose is a sit-back. None rotates the upper back with one hand planted.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a side-lying open book (side-lying with knees stacked, top arm sweeping open across the body while the trunk rotates).
curator.why: Side-Lying_Floor_Stretch is side-lying, but it is a lateral side-bend stretch: the top arm goes overhead and the wrist is pulled, with no thoracic rotation. Knee_Across_The_Body is a supine lumbar twist, with the knee pulled across a body lying on its back. Side_Jackknife is a side-lying oblique crunch with a leg raise. None shows the open-book rotation.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a tall-kneeling bodyweight trunk rotation with a reach.
curator.why: Torso_Rotation has the right action (trunk rotation with the arms extended) but is standing and holds an exercise ball. Pallof_Press_With_Rotation is standing with a cable. Kneeling_Cable_Crunch_With_Alternating_Oblique_Twists is a cable crunch down to all fours. Kneeling_Arm_Drill is a half-kneeling sprint arm swing. Landmine_180s (read) is standing with a barbell. Each one differs in body position, equipment or action.

name: Dead bug reach

curator.photoShows: Woman lying on her back. Frame 0: hips and knees at 90/90, both arms reaching straight up to the ceiling, back flat. Frame 1: same, but one leg extended long just above the floor while the arms stay vertical.
curator.why: The source is literally a dead bug: supine, bodyweight, 90/90 tabletop, one limb reaching long while the low back stays flat, alternating sides. That fits the cue ('exhale as the limb reaches; keep the low back from arching'), the regions (abdominals, hip flexors) and the dose (6 each side). Caveat: the source's version moves only the legs, and the arms stay vertical in both frames. If the app's 'reach' also means the opposite arm lowering overhead (the drill carries an 'overhead' tag), that arm reach is not pictured. The photo then shows the leg half, not a different drill. A verifier who treats the contralateral overhead arm reach as defining should downgrade this to none.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames, and the set-up matches the drill. She lies on her back on the floor with no equipment, hips and knees at 90/90 and both arms straight up toward the ceiling. Her lower back stays flat in both frames. In frame 1 one leg straightens long and stays just above the floor while the trunk holds still. That is 'the limb reaches; keep the low back from arching.' The listed regions (abdominals, hip flexors) are the ones loaded by the leg reach. The source alternates sides, which fits '6 each side.' One caveat: the arms stay vertical, so this is the leg-only dead bug, not the version where the opposite arm also reaches overhead. The cue only says 'the limb' (singular) and the regions are leg-focused, so the frames still teach the drill as cued. The 'overhead' tag looks like a session-selection tag, like its 'squat' and 'hinge' tags, not a described arm movement.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0 shows her on her back with hips and knees at 90/90 and both arms pointing straight up. In frame 1, one leg extends long just above the floor while both arms stay vertical. Only one leg moves; the arms never reach. The source describes this leg-only version (extend one leg, return, alternate). The app's item is named 'Dead bug reach' and is tagged 'overhead', so the arm reaching overhead while the ribs stay down is a defining part of it, and it is why the drill is chosen for overhead sessions. A coach usually runs the dead bug as the opposite arm reaching overhead together with the leg extending. Copying these frames gives a leg-only regression with the arms fixed, a cousin of the drill that never practices the overhead reach. There is no other dead bug source in the list. Strict rule: when in doubt, it is not a match.

finalReview: The reviewers split; a split is not a confirmation, so it has no photo.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a bird dog (quadruped with the opposite arm and leg reaching long at the same time).
curator.why: Rear_Leg_Raises is the closest. It is quadruped and extends one leg straight back, but both hands stay planted, so the defining contralateral arm reach ('heel to fingertips') is missing. Glute_Kickback is a bent-knee kickback with both hands down. Superman is prone, lifting all four limbs off the floor. Proposing Rear_Leg_Raises would be a near miss.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a high plank with one hand lifting to tap the opposite shoulder.
curator.why: Plank is a static forearm plank (frame 0 is a kneeling set-up), with no hand lift and no tap. Push_Up_to_Side_Plank shows only push-up top and bottom frames. Spider_Crawl is a push-up position with the knee driving to the elbow. Mountain_Climbers is hands-down leg running. None shows a hand leaving the floor to tap the shoulder.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a forearm side plank where the top arm threads under the body and rotates back open.
curator.why: Side_Bridge is a forearm side plank with the elbow under the shoulder, but the top hand stays on the hip. The frames show a hip drop and lift, with no reach-through or rotation, so the drill's defining action is missing. Push_Up_to_Side_Plank's frames show only a push-up, with no side plank pictured. Side_Jackknife is a side-lying crunch.

curator.photoShows: No source shows an unloaded bear crawl. The closest is Bear_Crawl_Sled_Drags: a man in a harness hitched to a sled, hands on the track, hips high and knees well bent, driving the sled.
curator.why: Bear_Crawl_Sled_Drags uses different equipment and a different action. It is a loaded sled drag with a harness and chain, and the hips sit high, not a free bear crawl with the knees floating just off the floor and opposite hand and foot moving. Spider_Crawl starts in a push-up position with the elbows bent and brings one knee out to the elbow. That is a different drill (plank with knee-to-elbow) and is not a quadruped crawl with knees hovering. No other source has a quadruped crawl.

curator.photoShows: Pallof_Press: a woman STANDING side-on to a cable tower, hands at the chest in frame 0 and arms pressed out in frame 1. Pallof_Press_With_Rotation: a man STANDING, the same press from a shoulder-height cable.
curator.why: Both Pallof sources are performed standing. The source instructions say 'feet positioned hip-width apart and knees slightly bent', and the photos show a standing stance. The drill is specifically TALL-KNEELING, so the body position differs (rule 1). Pallof_Press_With_Rotation also adds a torso twist, which the drill tells you to resist. No kneeling Pallof press exists in the source.

curator.photoShows: Standing_Cable_Wood_Chop: a man STANDING with feet shoulder-width apart, pulling a high cable down and across to the front knee. In frame 1 his back foot pivots and both knees bend.
curator.why: The only chop in the source is performed standing, and the instructions call for pivoting the back foot so the hips turn. The drill is HALF-KNEELING with the hips kept square, so the body position differs and so does the hip action. Standing_Cable_Lift is the reverse low-to-high pattern and is also standing. Kneeling_Cable_Crunch_With_Alternating_Oblique_Twists is a tall-kneeling cable crunch, not a chop. No half-kneeling chop exists.

curator.photoShows: Frame 0: a man bent over between two plate-loaded farmer handles, gripping them to pick them up. Frame 1: the same man walking upright toward the camera with one loaded handle in each hand at his sides, tall posture, mid-step.
curator.why: This is a bilateral loaded carry: the person stands tall, holds a load in each hand at the sides and walks a distance. That is the farmer carry pattern, with the farmer-carry implement (farmer handles), and frame 1 shows the 'walk tall, load close, ribs over hips' posture. The load here is heavy (strongman-style plates), but the rules say the load does not need to match, and the drill names no other implement. The step in frame 1 is a normal walking step, which fits the drill's 'Walk tall' cue and 20 m dose. Caveats for the verifier: the implement looks heavy and strongman-style, and there is no exaggerated knee-lift march. If 'march' means high-knee marching, this would fall short.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. Frame 0 shows a standing man hinged over two plate-loaded farmer handles at his sides, gripping them to lift. Frame 1 shows him upright and walking forward mid-step on flat ground. He holds one handle in each hand, close to his sides, with a tall trunk and his ribs stacked over his hips. Position (standing, then walking), implement (a loaded handle in each hand at the sides, which is a farmer carry) and action (walking a distance, not standing still and not running) all match the drill. The cue 'walk tall; keep the load close' is what frame 1 shows. The load is heavy rather than light, but the rule says load does not need to match while implement and pattern do. The cue describes plain walking, not an exaggerated high-knee march, and frame 1's normal stride fits that. No source in the database shows a lighter dumbbell or kettlebell carry. Someone copying these frames would pick up and carry the handles as the cue says.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0 shows a man bent over between two plate-loaded farmer handles, gripping them to pick them up. Frame 1 shows him upright and mid-step toward the camera, a handle in each hand at his sides, torso tall and ribs stacked over the hips. Between the frames he picks the load up and then walks with it. That is the farmer carry, with its namesake implement. The drill's cue ('walk tall; keep the load close, ribs over hips') and its 20 m dose describe walking a distance, which matches frame 1, not marching on the spot. The photo uses a heavy strongman load where the drill says 'light', but the load does not have to match. The drill names no specific implement, and farmer handles are the standard one. Someone copying these frames would do a farmer carry walk. Minor point: frame 0 is the pickup, not the carry, but it is the normal setup for this drill and does not teach a different movement.

curator.photoShows: Medicine_Ball_Scoop_Throw: a man in a semisquat holding a ball at knee height (frame 0), then extending onto his toes with arms straight overhead, releasing the ball backward (frame 1).
curator.why: The drill is a rotational scoop, done 6 each side and tagged rotation and obliques: a side-on scoop toss. The source's Scoop Throw is a two-handed, front-facing triple-extension throw backward over the head, with no rotation and no sides, so the action differs (rule 3). Medicine_Ball_Full_Twist is a back-to-back partner hand-off twist, not a scoop. Backward_Medicine_Ball_Throw, Chest Pass and Slam are different patterns. No rotational scoop toss exists in the source.

name: Split-stance row rehearsal

curator.photoShows: A man in a wide split (lunge) stance facing a low cable, torso leaning forward, free hand near the front thigh. Frame 0: the working arm is extended toward the pulley with the shoulder reached forward. Frame 1: the elbow is drawn back beside the torso and the handle is at the hip.
curator.why: This is a single-arm row from a split stance, done one side at a time, with a cable as the light load. That matches the stance, the laterality and the horizontal pull of a split-stance row rehearsal, and the drill names no specific implement. Caveats for the verifier: the Shotgun Row adds wrist supination and a forward shoulder reach at the start, and the torso leans further forward than a typical rehearsal. The drill's cue says to resist trunk rotation, while this photo shows slight shoulder opening. Kneeling_Single-Arm_High_Pulley_Row was rejected because it is kneeling with a high pulley. One-Arm_Kettlebell_Row, Alternating_Kettlebell_Row, One-Arm_Long_Bar_Row and Bent_Over_One-Arm_Long_Bar_Row were rejected because they are bent-over rows with the feet roughly level, not split stance.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. A man stands in a wide split stance facing a low cable pulley and rows one arm at a time, which matches '8 each side'. The front knee is bent and the rear leg is extended, and his torso leans forward with the trunk square. The working arm is on the same side as the rear leg, so the stance is opposite to the rowing arm, which is the standard set-up. The free hand rests near the front thigh. Frame 0: the working arm is long toward the pulley. Frame 1: the elbow is pulled back beside the ribs with the handle at the lower chest or hip, and the trunk faces about the same way as in frame 0, so it shows the anti-rotation intent. The drill names no implement and asks only for a light load, so a single-handle low cable fits. Two small differences from a generic split-stance row: the shotgun row adds a turn of the palm upward during the pull, and frame 0 lets the shoulder reach slightly forward. Neither changes the body position, support or rowing pattern, so copying these frames gives a correct split-stance row.

I viewed both frames and zoomed in on the torso. In frame 0 his back faces the camera: he is hinged deeply forward in a very wide lunge-depth split stance, and the working shoulder reaches far forward toward a low cable, so his trunk is turned toward the pulley. In frame 1 the trunk has turned clearly back open: his near side and chest now face the camera, the elbow is pulled behind the ribs and the palm is turned up. The source's instructions describe a 'shoulder forward' start that ends with the shoulder pulled back, so the row is a reach, row and rotate. The drill's cue asks for the opposite: 'resist trunk rotation while rowing'. Someone copying these frames would twist the trunk toward the cable and back on every rep, which is the shotgun row, a relative of the drill, not the anti-rotation split-stance row it names. The extreme forward lean and the hand resting on the front knee also go beyond a light split-stance row rehearsal.

finalReview: The reviewers split; a split is not a confirmation, so it has no photo.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a full straight-arm pass-through. Chest_And_Front_Of_Shoulder_Stretch: the man stands holding a body bar with a wide grip at his hips (frame 0), then lifts it to just above and behind his head with the elbows clearly bent at about 90-120 degrees (frame 1). Round_The_World_Shoulder_Stretch: the bar is held behind the hips and only lifted slightly backward (shoulder extension behind the back).
curator.why: The drill is a wide-grip stick moved with long arms from the front of the hips, over the head and behind the back. Chest_And_Front_Of_Shoulder_Stretch comes closest but shows only the first half, and its top frame has the elbows strongly bent with the bar parked behind the head. That would teach a bent-arm behind-the-head stretch, not a pass-through. Round_The_World shows only a small behind-the-back lift. Neither shows the drill on its own, and splicing frames from two sources is not allowed. Near miss, so none.

curator.photoShows: Standing athlete holding a light band in both hands. Frame 0: arms straight in front at shoulder height with the band slack. Frame 1: arms pulled out to the sides with straight elbows, the band stretched across at chest level.
curator.why: Same position (standing), same equipment (handheld band, not anchored), same action (horizontal straight-arm pull-apart from the front to the sides) and same regions (rear delts, upper back). Back_Flyes_-_With_Bands was rejected because its band is anchored to a rack post, which makes it a different set-up.

reviewers.reason: Viewed both frames. The athlete stands square with feet about hip width and holds a light red loop band in both hands with an overhand grip. Frame 0: arms straight out in front at shoulder height with the hands about shoulder width apart, and the band only slightly taut. Frame 1: arms opened straight out to the sides in a T, elbows extended, band stretched across the front of the upper chest and shoulders. The shoulders sit level and are not shrugged toward the ears. The position (standing), equipment (light band, no anchor), action (horizontal abduction to the sides, not overhead or diagonal), laterality (both arms together) and range (full opening to the chest) all match a standard band pull-apart. The photo does not explicitly show the shoulder blades sliding down, but nothing in it contradicts the cue.

I viewed both frames. The athlete stands with a light red band held overhand in both hands. In frame 0 the arms are straight out in front at shoulder height with the hands about shoulder-width apart. In frame 1 the arms are pulled straight out to the sides in a reverse-fly arc, elbows still straight, and the band is stretched across the front of the shoulders and chest. The movement is a horizontal pull-apart with no rowing, no overhead pass-through and no rotation, and the shoulders stay down rather than shrugged at the finish. Someone copying these two frames would do a band pull-apart as the cue describes. The implement (band), standing position, two-arm action and body part (rear delts and upper back) all match.

curator.photoShows: No source shows forearms or arms sliding up a wall. The only wall sources are calf stretches against a wall, One_Arm_Against_Wall (a static lat lean with a bent arm on the wall), Handstand_Push-Ups and Linear_Acceleration_Wall_Drill.
curator.why: No source has a wall slide, i.e. arms gliding up and down a wall for serratus and lower-trap control. One_Arm_Against_Wall is a static one-arm lat stretch leaning into the wall: a different action and a different drill.

curator.photoShows: Pushups shows a standard push-up with the elbows bending to bring the chest to the floor. Barbell_Incline_Shoulder_Raise shows scapular protraction, but lying back on an incline bench with a loaded barbell.
curator.why: A push-up plus is done in a straight-arm plank and moves only the shoulder blades (protraction). Pushups shows elbow flexion, the opposite of the cue 'without bending the elbows'. Barbell_Incline_Shoulder_Raise has the right scapular action but the wrong position (supine on an incline) and the wrong implement (barbell). No source shows the plus in a plank.

curator.photoShows: Athlete hanging from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip and knees bent. Frame 0: passive dead hang with the shoulders shrugged up around the ears. Frame 1: the body is raised a few inches by depressing and retracting the shoulder blades, with the elbows still straight.
curator.why: Same position (hanging), same equipment (pull-up bar), same action (scapular depression only, elbows long) and same regions (lower traps, lats). This is the named drill itself.

reviewers.reason: Viewed both frames, shot from behind and slightly to the side. The athlete hangs from a pull-up bar in a power rack with an overhand grip at about shoulder width, knees bent and feet off the floor. Frame 0: passive dead hang, arms fully straight, head sunk between the arms and shoulders elevated around the ears. Frame 1: the torso and head have risen a few inches, the shoulders are pulled down away from the ears and the shoulder blades are drawn down and back, while the elbows stay essentially straight (at most a trace of softness in one arm, with no visible elbow flexion or pulling). The position (hanging), support (fixed bar, overhand grip), action (scapular depression only, not a partial pull-up), and short range shown all match the drill as cued: 'Move only through the shoulder blades; keep the elbows long.'

I viewed both frames, plus a zoomed crop of the upper body. The athlete hangs from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, knees bent to clear the floor. In frame 0 it is a passive dead hang: the head sits low between the arms and the shoulders are shrugged up toward the ears. In frame 1 the head and trunk sit a few inches higher, the neck is visible, and the shoulder blades are pulled down and back. Both elbows stay essentially straight, so the rise comes from the shoulder blades and not from bending the arms, which would make it a partial pull-up. Someone copying the frames would do a hanging scapular pull-up that moves only through the shoulder blades with long elbows, as the cue says. The bar, the hanging position and the scapular depression all match.

curator.photoShows: No source shows arms raised overhead against a wall and lifted off it. Upward_Stretch shows a free-standing overhead reach with no wall, and One_Arm_Against_Wall shows a static lat lean.
curator.why: The drill needs a wall as support and a lift-off of the arms from it in flexion. Upward_Stretch has no wall and no lift-off, and is a static overhead stretch. One_Arm_Against_Wall is a different action (leaning into a bent arm for a lat stretch). No source matches.

curator.photoShows: Shoulder_Circles shows a standing shoulder roll with the arms at the sides. Cat_Stretch shows a quadruped spinal round (flexion). Hip_Circles_prone shows a quadruped hip circle with one leg lifted and circled.
curator.why: The drill is a circle of the shoulder blades while on all fours. Shoulder_Circles has the right action but the wrong position (standing). Cat_Stretch has the right position but the wrong action (whole-spine flexion, not a scapular circle). Hip_Circles_prone has the right position but the wrong body part (hip). None of them is this drill.

curator.photoShows: Standing side-on to a band anchored on a rack post at elbow height, elbow pinned to the side (with a small pad), forearm at 90 degrees. Frame 0: hand across the front of the torso. Frame 1: forearm rotated outward past the body line with the elbow still at the side.
curator.why: Same standing position, same equipment (a band anchored at elbow height), same action (a single-arm external rotation with the elbow pinned and the torso still) and same body part (rotator cuff). This is exactly the drill the cue describes. The dumbbell side-lying External_Rotation and External_Rotation_with_Cable both use the wrong implement.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames and enlarged crops of the arm. He stands front-on with his right side toward a rack post. A light band is anchored to the post at elbow height and runs horizontally to a handle in his LEFT hand, so the working arm is on the side away from the anchor, which is correct for external rotation. A yellow/black pad is clamped between his left elbow and ribs in both frames, and the elbow stays at 90 degrees against his side. Frame 0: the forearm points across the front of his torso, with the hand at his midline. Frame 1: the forearm has rotated out to his body line and slightly past it, the elbow still pinned and the pad still in place. The torso stays square to the camera with no trunk rotation in either frame, which matches the cue. Standing, band, elbow pinned at the side, single arm (so the '10 each side' dose works) and the range is the standard internal-to-external rotation. Someone copying these frames would do a band external rotation as cued.

Viewed and enlarged both frames. The athlete stands front-on and works the LEFT arm. The band is anchored on the opposite (right-side) rack post at elbow height, and a pad is clamped between the left elbow and the ribs. Frame 0: forearm at 90 degrees with the hand across the front of the torso. Frame 1: the same forearm has swung out past the body line while the elbow stays pinned on the pad. The only change between frames is forearm rotation about a fixed upper arm. The shoulders and torso stay square, so there is no trunk rotation and the 'avoid rotating the whole torso' cue holds. Copying it gives standing band external rotation, the drill named. Showing one side is fine for '10 each side'. There is no different body position, support or action to object to.

curator.photoShows: Face_Pull: standing at a cable column with a rope. Frame 0: arms extended toward the stack. Frame 1: rope pulled to the face with elbows high and wide, but the forearms are close to horizontal and the hands sit in front of the eyes and nose. They are not beside the ears.
curator.why: The drill is named for its external-rotation finish, and the cue says to finish with the hands beside the ears (forearms vertical). The only face pull photo shows a plain face pull with almost no external rotation at the end, so the photo would teach a finish that is missing the drill's defining part. That makes it the base movement for a named variation the source does not have. Reverse_Flyes_With_External_Rotation is a prone incline-bench dumbbell fly, and Cuban Press is an upright row to a press, so both are different drills.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a bodyweight prone Y raise. Superman: prone on a floor mat, lifting both arms and the legs together. Lower_Back_Curl: prone back extension with the arms at the sides. Straight_Raises_on_Incline_Bench: prone on an incline bench, raising a loaded barbell forward with a narrow grip. Dumbbell_Scaption: standing raise with dumbbells, thumbs up.
curator.why: A prone Y raise is lying face down, bodyweight, with the arms in a Y and thumbs up, in a small range. Superman adds a leg and chest lift and works the lower back. Lower_Back_Curl is a spinal extension with the arms down. The incline-bench raise uses a barbell at a narrow width, so it cannot form a Y. Scaption is standing and uses dumbbells. Each one differs in position, equipment or action.

curator.photoShows: Standing front-on with both arms straight out to the sides. Frame 0: arms parallel to the floor. Frame 1: arms a little higher at another point of the circle.
curator.why: Same standing position, no equipment, same action (outstretched arms making circles that can be enlarged) and same body part (shoulders). The source has you make small circles and then reverse them, which fits '8 each direction' and the cue about growing the circle. Shoulder_Circles is a shoulder roll with the arms down, a different drill.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. He stands tall facing the camera, feet together, with no equipment, and both arms straight out to the sides with palms down. Frame 0: arms parallel to the floor, perpendicular to the torso. Frame 1: both arms a little above horizontal, another point on a small circle. That is the source's arm-circle set-up: both arms out to the sides, small circles of about a foot. It fits a standing, unloaded, two-arm shoulder circle done '8 each direction'. The small range shown suits the cue, which starts small and grows the circle only as far as is comfortable. Two stills cannot draw a circle, so the name carries the circling. The position, support (none), body part (whole arm from the shoulder) and laterality (both arms together) all match, and nothing shown would teach a different drill.

Viewed both frames. Standing front-on, no equipment, both arms straight out to the sides with palms down. Frame 0: arms level with the floor. Frame 1: both arms raised roughly 20 degrees higher. Two stills of a circle can only show two points on its path. These are two points of the source's small straight-arm circle (about 1 ft across, reversed after about 10 s). They are not a different drill: not a shoulder shrug circle (Shoulder_Circles), not fingertips-on-shoulders elbow circles (Elbow_Circles), and not a static hold. The name and the cue 'grow the circle' supply the circling motion. Starting small from the arms-out position and enlarging matches the source's own pattern. The body position, support and moving joint (the whole arm at the shoulder) are the same as 'Controlled arm circle'. This is the only straight-arm circle source.

curator.photoShows: Single-arm landmine press: a loaded barbell anchored in a landmine at the floor, athlete standing in a wide or staggered stance. Frame 0: bar end held at the shoulder in one hand with the knees slightly bent. Frame 1: the same arm pressed fully along the bar's arc, body leaning into the bar.
curator.why: The implement (a barbell in a landmine), the standing stance and the single-arm press along the bar's arc all match a landmine press done 6 each side. The task allows a light rehearsal to be matched by a photo of the lift with any load. Caveats: the source is the explosive 'jammer' version with leg drive, and frame 1 shows a large forward lean with the head ducked. A coach cueing 'ribs stacked' would want a little less lean. Landmine_Linear_Jammer is not a match because it is two hands on a handle attachment from a squat (a thruster pattern).

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames and a side-by-side crop of the athlete. The implement is a barbell anchored at the floor in a landmine-type base on a rack, with a plate on the free end. He grips the bare sleeve end in one hand (right). There is no handle attachment, and the other hand is a loose fist at his chest, so it is single-arm, which fits '6 each side'. He stands in a wide, staggered stance. Frame 0: the bar end is at the right shoulder, beside the face, with the knees only softly bent. Frame 1: the arm is locked out up and forward along the bar's arc, and the body leans into the bar. The legs look almost the same in both frames. There is no visible dip-and-drive, so despite the 'jammer' name this pair reads as the strict standing single-arm landmine press. The app already uses this pair for Landmine Press and Single-Arm Standing Landmine Press. The finish lean is forward, along the press line, not a lumbar arch or rib flare, so it does not contradict 'ribs stacked'. The full reach at lockout shows the serratus range the drill targets. The landmine, single arm, standing stance and press arc all match a light landmine press rehearsal. Caveat: the forward lean with the head ducked under the arm in frame 1 is more than ideal, so the cue should keep 'ribs stacked'.

Viewed the pair and enlarged each raw frame. The barbell sits in a floor landmine base. The athlete stands in a staggered stance facing the anchor and holds the bar end in one hand. Frame 0: bar end at the shoulder and face, other fist at the chest, knees almost straight. Frame 1: the same arm is pressed to full extension along the bar's arc, reaching long, with the trunk leaning into the bar. I looked specifically for the jammer's defining dip and drive (an explosive knee and hip extension). The legs are nearly straight in both frames, so copying this gives a strict single-arm standing landmine press, not a push press or thruster. That is consistent with the project's earlier rematch: this pair already illustrates Landmine Press and Single-Arm Standing Landmine Press, and it was withdrawn from Landmine Push Press for lacking a dip. The drill is a light rehearsal of that same lift with the same implement, one arm per rep ('6 each side'), and the long lockout reach also serves the serratus region. Caveat: the frame-1 lockout leans the trunk well forward with the head ducked under the arm. There is no lumbar arch or rib flare, so it does not contradict 'ribs stacked', but it is a deeper lean than ideal. The other landmine sources do not fit: Landmine_Linear_Jammer is a two-handle squat-to-press and Landmine_180s is a rotation. Implement, support, laterality and press-along-the-arc action all match.

curator.photoShows: Barbell Romanian deadlift, facing the camera, overhand grip. Frame 0: hips pushed back, knees slightly bent, flat back, bar just below the knees. Frame 1: standing tall with the bar at the hips.
curator.why: A barbell hip hinge with the hips moving back and soft knees is exactly the pattern of an empty-bar hinge rehearsal. The implement and pattern match; the source's plates are only load, which the rules do not require to match. Stiff-Legged_Barbell_Deadlift lowers the bar to the floor, which is less of a hips-back hinge. Good_Morning puts the bar on the back, a different hinge.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The implement is a straight barbell held overhand, just outside the thighs. He stands front-on, feet about hip width, with no box, platform or other support. Frame 0: hips pushed back, knees only slightly bent, shins near vertical, a flat back, and the bar just below the knees, a clean hip hinge. Frame 1: standing tall with the bar at the hips. That is the barbell hip-hinge pattern the rehearsal names, and the rehearsal rule allows a heavier load: the photo has plates loaded, not an empty bar, but the implement and pattern match. The app already uses this pair for Barbell Hip Hinge. Someone copying these frames would push the hips back with soft knees and a flat back holding a bar, which is the cue.

Viewed both frames. A barbell held overhand with both hands, feet hip-width, facing the camera. One frame is the bottom of the hinge: hips pushed back, knees only softly bent with near-vertical shins, flat back, and the bar just below the knees with the arms straight. The other frame is standing tall with the bar at the hips. The movement between them is a pure hip hinge, hips back and forward without squatting. That is exactly 'feel the hips move back' for the hamstrings and spine regions. The implement (a straight barbell held with both hands) and the pattern match. Plates are loaded on the bar, but under the rehearsal rule the load does not need to match, only the implement and pattern. Same position, support and action as the drill.

curator.photoShows: Kettlebell held by the horns at the chest, facing the camera. Frame 0: standing tall. Frame 1: deep squat at the bottom, chest up, elbows inside the knees.
curator.why: Same implement (a kettlebell held goblet-style as the counterbalance), same pattern (a bodyweight-stance squat to a deep bottom position) and same regions. The source also says to pause at the bottom, which matches the cue.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. He faces the camera holding one kettlebell by the horns, close to his chest, with no other support. His feet are about shoulder width, toes slightly out. Frame 0: standing tall with the bell at the chest. Frame 1: a deep squat with the hips below the knees, chest up and the bell still at the chest, elbows inside the knees. That is the stable bottom position the cue asks him to pause in. The implement (a light counterbalance held goblet-style), the standing two-foot stance and the squat pattern all match a light goblet squat rehearsal.

Viewed both frames. A single kettlebell held by the horns close to the chest, standing front-on with a shoulder-width-plus stance and no other support. Frame 0: standing tall. Frame 1: deep squat with hamstrings near the calves, chest and head up, and elbows inside the knees. The action is a squat down to a held bottom position. The source itself says to pause at the bottom and push the knees out with the elbows, which matches the cue 'pause briefly in a stable bottom position'. The implement (a kettlebell as a front counterbalance) and the pattern match the light goblet squat rehearsal. The load is a light bell, which fits 'light counterbalance'.

curator.photoShows: Barbell_Bench_Press_-_Medium_Grip: lying on a flat bench, bar locked out in frame 0 and touching the mid-chest in frame 1. Standing_Military_Press: standing, bar at the collarbone in frame 0 and locked out overhead in frame 1.
curator.why: The drill does not say which press it is. Its regions are chest and shoulders, and in client/src/lib/preTrainingMobility.ts it is tagged both horizontalPush and verticalPush, so the app shows it before bench days and before overhead-press days. Either photo would show the wrong bar path and position for one of those uses, which is a near miss. If the drill is split or renamed, the bench press photo fits an 'empty-bar bench press rehearsal' and the military press photo fits an 'empty-bar overhead press rehearsal'.

curator.photoShows: The source has no band row. Seated_Cable_Rows: seated at a cable stack with a V handle. Upright_Row_-_With_Bands: standing on a band, pulling the handles vertically up to the chin.
curator.why: The drill is a horizontal row with a band. The only band pull in the source that resembles a row is an upright row, which is a vertical pull to the chin and a different action. Seated cable rows and suspended or inverted rows have the right action but different equipment and support (a cable machine, straps, a bar). Band_Pull_Apart and Back_Flyes_-_With_Bands are straight-arm abduction, not rows.

curator.photoShows: One_Handed_Hang: hanging from a chin-up bar with one hand, feet on the floor, other hand on the hip; both frames are the same hold. Scapular_Pull-Up: two-hand overhand hang in frame 0 and an active scapular depression lifting the body slightly in frame 1, knees bent and feet off the floor.
curator.why: A dead hang is a two-hand, passive, static hang with optional foot support. One_Handed_Hang has foot support but uses one arm, which makes it a different, unilateral lat stretch. Scapular_Pull-Up shows a dead hang only in frame 0; frame 1 shows an active pulling movement, and the drill is a hold, not a pull. Pullups and Hanging_Leg_Raise also include large movements.

curator.photoShows: A man stands with his feet shoulder-width apart, no equipment, arms held away from his sides with the elbows nearly straight. In frame 0 the arms are raised about 40 degrees and both wrists are bent back with the palms open and the fingers pointing out. In frame 1 the arms are lower and the hands hang down and out, bent the other way. The two frames are two points on a circle drawn by the wrists.
curator.why: This is the source's own Wrist Circles. Its instructions are to stand, hold the arms out and keep everything still except the wrists, which draw circles. That matches the drill on every point: standing position, no equipment, a circling action (not a hold) and the wrist as the moving joint. One caveat: the instructions call for arms at shoulder height in a T, but the arms are lower in both frames and lower still in frame 1. The arm height changes a little between frames, but the elbows stay extended and the visible change is at the wrists. Nothing else in the source shows wrist circles.

reviewers.reason: I looked at both frames, including enlarged crops. The set-up matches the drill: he stands with feet about shoulder-width apart, uses no equipment, and holds both arms out to the sides with the elbows extended in both frames. Only the wrist position changes in a way that matters. In frame 0 both wrists are extended, with palms facing out and fingers pointing up and out. In frame 1 both wrists are flexed, with the hands hanging and fingers pointing down. These are the extension and flexion points of a wrist circle, and the elbows do not bend, which fits the cue 'move through the wrist, not the elbow.' Both wrists are shown, so nothing is wrong on laterality. Two small issues are not enough to refute. First, the arms sit lower than the source's instructed shoulder-height T: about 40 degrees in frame 0 and about 25 degrees in frame 1. That means the shoulder drops a little between frames, though the elbows stay straight. Second, two frames cannot show that the path is circular. The app's drill does not name an arm height, and this is the source's own Wrist Circles photo of the same standing, both-wrist drill, so someone copying it would do a standing wrist circle.

I viewed both frames, including zoomed crops with a grid. He is standing, with no equipment, and his arms are held out and down from his sides with the elbows a little bent. Between the frames the hand turns about 90 to 120 degrees around the wrist. In frame 0 the hand is bent back, palm forward and fingers pointing out. In frame 1 the hand hangs down with the fingers pointing at the floor. The forearms and elbows barely move: the wrists drop only slightly and the elbow angle is almost the same. So the motion comes from the wrist, as the cue 'Move through the wrist, not the elbow' asks. These are the top and bottom of a wrist circle from the source that is itself called 'Wrist Circles', and it is the only source for this movement. Two caveats. The arms sit lower than the T position in the source's text, but the drill does not set an arm height. Two frames cannot draw the circle, but the drill's name supplies it. Copying the photos gives the named drill, not a wrist flap or an arm swing.

curator.photoShows: A man on all fours on a mat, palms flat with the fingers pointing back toward his knees. In frame 0 his hips are over his knees and his shoulders over his hands. In frame 1 he has shifted his weight back toward his heels, with his shoulders behind his hands, which bends the wrists further back and stretches the forearms.
curator.why: The position matches (all fours, palms flat, no equipment), the body part matches (wrists and forearms), and the two frames show a gradual shift of bodyweight across the hands, which is the range of a rock. The source calls it a static stretch, but it is done in the same position and the frames show the full rocking range, so it meets the rule for using a static stretch photo for a mobility drill. Caveat for the orchestrator: the photo shows the fingers-back hand position, a recognised variant of the quadruped wrist rock in which the person rocks backward. The default version, implied by the cue's 'turn the hands out if needed', points the fingers forward and rocks forward. If the app wants fingers forward only, reject this match. No source shows the fingers-forward version.

reviewers.reason: The enlarged crops show the wrong hand set-up for this drill. In both frames the palms are flat with the fingers pointing back toward the knees, which is a reverse-hand position. Between frames he shifts his weight back toward his heels, moving the shoulders from over or in front of the hands to behind them. That is the reverse-hand forearm flexor stretch. The app's quadruped wrist rock is tagged horizontalPush, and its cue offers 'turn the hands out or elevate them' as a regression. That is the standard regression for the fingers-forward, push-up-style wrist rock, where the shoulders rock forward past the hands to load wrist extension. Someone copying these frames would turn the hands around and rock backward. That is the opposite hand orientation and the opposite rock direction, and it is a harder end-range position (wrist extension with the forearm turned palm-up and the elbow locked) than the gentle push-prep rock with a regression that this dose and cue describe. The source is also a 20-30 second static hold, not repeated rocks. Position (quadruped, on a mat, no equipment, both hands) matches, but the hand placement does not. I found no fingers-forward quadruped wrist source in the list.

Zoomed crops of the hands in both frames show the palms flat with the fingers clearly pointing BACK toward the knees, so the heel of the hand faces forward. The movement between frames is a sit-back toward the heels: the hips move behind the knees and the shoulders move behind the hands, so the forearm tilts back over the fingers. Copying these frames gives the reverse-hand kneeling wrist-flexor stretch (rocking back on reversed hands). The standard 'Quadruped wrist rock' coaches put the fingers pointing forward and rock the shoulders forward over the hands. That is the version the app means: the drill is tagged horizontalPush to prepare the wrists for push-ups and bench, and its cue offers 'turn the hands out or elevate them' as the way to ease off. The photo shows the fingers-back hand position, which is the hardest on the wrist flexors and elbows. It is not mentioned in the cue and is the opposite of the easier options it offers. The hand direction and the rock direction both differ, so this is a cousin drill for the same region and would teach the wrong hand placement. The source is also a static 20-30 second hold, not a rock.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows this drill. The drill is done one side at a time ('each side'): the arm is extended and the other hand gently takes the relaxed fingers back to bend the wrist in small gliding movements.
curator.why: Closest candidates: (1) Kneeling_Forearm_Stretch bends the wrists back but on all fours, with both hands at once and the bodyweight as the load, which is a different position and set-up from a one-arm, hand-assisted glide. (2) Seated_One-Arm_Dumbbell_Palms-Down_Wrist_Curl is seated with the forearm on the thigh and lifts a dumbbell, so it is a loaded strength curl, not a glide. (3) Side_Wrist_Pull is a cross-body back and shoulder stretch in which one hand only grips the other wrist. (4) Wrist_Circles circles the wrist. The source has no standing or seated hand-assisted wrist extension stretch.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows this drill. The drill: the arm is held out with the elbow straight but not locked, and the other hand gently presses the back of the hand to bend the wrist forward, repeated on each side.
curator.why: No source photo shows a hand-assisted wrist flexion stretch or glide. Closest candidates: (1) Seated_One-Arm_Dumbbell_Palms-Down_Wrist_Curl and the palms-up version are seated, with the elbow bent over the thigh, lifting a dumbbell, so the position, equipment and action are all different. (2) Wrist_Rotations_with_Straight_Bar is standing with a barbell, rolling the wrists alternately. (3) Side_Wrist_Pull is a shoulder and back stretch. (4) Kneeling_Forearm_Stretch bends the wrist back on all fours, which is the opposite direction.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows this drill. The drill: the elbow is bent and the palm turns up and down by rotating the forearm, with no load, done on each side.
curator.why: Closest candidates: (1) Dumbbell_Lying_Pronation shows him face down on a bench with the upper arm out and the elbow bent at 90 degrees, rotating a dumbbell forward. The rotation is at the shoulder and the forearm does not rotate. (2) Dumbbell_Lying_Supination is the same set-up lying on his side, again rotating at the shoulder. (3) Zottman_Curl turns the palm at the top of a dumbbell curl, so it is an elbow-bending curl with load. (4) Wrist_Rotations_with_Straight_Bar rolls the wrists back and forth on a barbell, which is not a palm rotation. None shows an unloaded forearm rotation.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows this drill. The drill: a rubber band is looped around the fingertips and the fingers spread against it to open the hand fully.
curator.why: No source exercise loops a band around the fingers, and none spreads the fingers against resistance. Closest candidates: (1) Finger_Curls is seated, letting a barbell roll down the fingers and curling it back up, which works the finger flexors against load. (2) Standing_Olympic_Plate_Hand_Squeeze holds a plate by its rim, a grip or flexion move. Both use different equipment and the opposite action. None of the source's band exercises involves the hand.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows a push-up with a clap. Plyo_Push-up (withdrawn) shows only a plain push-up, bottom then top, with the hands on the floor. Clock_Push-Up shows a push-up with a lateral shift and no clap. Drop_Push shows hands on two boxes.
curator.why: The source has no clap push-up. Plyo_Push-up was withdrawn and cannot be proposed again; its instructions only mention claps as an option, and neither frame shows the hands off the floor or clapping. Clock_Push-Up is a lateral 'clock' hop around a circle, Drop_Push drops from boxes, and Plyo_Kettlebell_Pushups switch hands over a kettlebell. Each is a different plyometric push-up variation.

curator.photoShows: Every barbell bent-over row in the source keeps the bar hanging at mid-shin or knee height between reps, never resting on the floor with the torso parallel. Bent_Over_Barbell_Row (withdrawn) uses an overhand grip and Reverse_Grip_Bent-Over_Rows an underhand grip, both with the bar hanging.
curator.why: A Pendlay row is a dead-stop row: the bar returns to the floor every rep and the torso stays near parallel. No source shows that. Bent_Over_Barbell_Row was withdrawn for this reason. Reverse_Grip_Bent-Over_Rows also has the bar hanging and uses a supinated grip. Smith_Machine_Bent_Over_Row is a machine, and the Long Bar/T-bar rows use a landmine-style bar. Showing the base movement for a named variation the source lacks is not allowed.

curator.photoShows: Lying_Cambered_Barbell_Row: a man lies prone on a standard-height flat bench with his feet up on it and rows a cambered (bent-centre) barbell. In frame 0 the plates rest on the floor under the bench; in frame 1 the bar is pulled up to the bench. Incline_Bench_Pull (withdrawn) is chest-supported on an incline bench.
curator.why: This is the closest candidate, but it is not a seal row as specified: the bench is not raised, so the weight starts resting on the floor rather than hanging free, and the implement is a specialty cambered bar rather than a straight barbell or dumbbells. That makes it a separate named variation (the source calls it 'Lying Cambered Barbell Row') with different support height, start position and implement. Incline_Bench_Pull was withdrawn and Dumbbell_Incline_Row is also on an incline. Lying_T-Bar_Row is a machine, and Straight_Bar_Bench_Mid_Rows is a standing row on top of a bench. Chose none over a near miss.

curator.photoShows: V-Bar_Pullup: a V-bar (cable row handle) is draped over a straight pull-up bar, and the man grips it with his hands almost touching and his knees bent. Frame 0 is the top position with his chin near the bar; frame 1 is the hang. Pullups (withdrawn) shows angled handles with the palms forward.
curator.why: The source has no pull-up on parallel neutral handles at about shoulder width. V-Bar_Pullup does give palms-facing hands, but it uses a different attachment (a V-handle hung over a straight bar, which its own instructions call a stand-in when the station has no neutral handles) and a very close, hands-touching grip. That is a separate close-grip V-bar variation, and the attachment would teach the wrong setup. Pullups was withdrawn. Chin-Up (supinated), Mixed_Grip_Chin, Weighted_Pull_Ups, Rocky/Side_To_Side chins, Gironda_Sternum_Chins and Band_Assisted_Pull-Up are all non-neutral grips by their instructions. Chose none over a near miss.

curator.photoShows: Standing split squat with the rear foot's instep resting on a flat bench behind and a dumbbell hanging in each hand. Frame 0: standing tall at the top. Frame 1: descended with the front thigh near parallel and the rear knee lowered toward the floor.
curator.why: This is exactly a Bulgarian split squat: rear foot elevated on a bench, bilateral dumbbells (free weights), single-leg knee-dominant squat, and an upright torso. The source instructions state 'staggered stance with the rear foot elevated'. It replaces the withdrawn Split_Squats, which had the rear foot on the floor. One_Leg_Barbell_Squat is also a rear-foot-elevated split squat, but with a back-racked barbell; the dumbbell version is the more standard presentation.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. Frame 0: the athlete stands in a fixed staggered stance. The instep of the rear foot rests on a flat bench behind him, the front foot is flat on the floor well in front, the torso is upright and a dumbbell hangs at each side. Frame 1: the same stance and support, lowered into the split. The front thigh is close to parallel, the rear knee drops toward the floor under the hip and the dumbbells still hang at the sides. Checked for set-up: it is a rear-foot-elevated split squat (Bulgarian), with the rear foot raised on the bench, not on the floor. That was the reason Split_Squats (#173's withdrawn photo) failed, and this photo fixes it. It is unilateral with a fixed stance, not a stepping lunge. The implement is dumbbells, which fits 'Free weights', and the range is full. The source's own instructions describe the same set-up: rear foot elevated, dumbbells hanging at the sides, descend and drive back up. Someone copying these frames would perform a Bulgarian split squat.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0: the athlete stands tall in a fixed staggered stance with the instep of his rear foot resting on a flat bench behind him and a dumbbell hanging at each side. Frame 1: he holds the same stance. The front knee and hip have flexed until the front thigh is near parallel, the rear knee has dropped toward the floor, the torso stays upright and the dumbbells still hang. Between the frames the hips move straight down and up over a planted front foot. Nothing steps or jumps, the bench foot stays where it is, and there is no forward travel. So the action is a stationary, rear-foot-elevated, single-leg-dominant squat with dumbbells, which is a Bulgarian split squat. The source's instructions describe the same thing ('rear foot elevated', dumbbells at the sides, descend, drive through the heel to return). The implement is a free weight, which matches 'Free weights'. Someone copying these frames would do a Bulgarian split squat, not a lunge or a floor split squat. The withdrawn source was Split_Squats, a bodyweight jumping split with the rear foot on the floor. This is a different source, and it fixes exactly that problem.

curator.photoShows: One-Arm_Kettlebell_Swings (withdrawn) is single-arm. Vertical_Swing is a dumbbell swung overhead with a jump. Kettlebell_Pass_Between_The_Legs hands a kettlebell from one hand to the other between the legs.
curator.why: No source shows a two-hand kettlebell swing. One-Arm_Kettlebell_Swings was withdrawn as single-arm. reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The athlete stands centred in a cable crossover with feet about shoulder-width apart. He holds a single handle in each hand with the palms up, and both pulleys are set above shoulder height. Frame 0: his arms are straight out to the sides at about shoulder height in a T, with the cables running level to the high pulleys. Frame 1: the upper arms stay in that position and both elbows bend, bringing the hands beside the head in a double-biceps pose. This is exactly the 'standing two-pulley curl' that the withdrawal note for #339 named as the right exercise. The withdrawn High_Cable_Curls photo was taken lying on a bench, so this is a different source and fixes that fault. The equipment is a cable, the body position is standing, the attachment is single handles, both arms work, the upper arms stay abducted at shoulder height and the action is elbow flexion only. All of these match a high cable curl. Someone copying these frames would perform a high cable curl.

I viewed both frames. The athlete stands centred in a cable crossover, holding a single D-handle in each hand from pulleys set above shoulder height. Frame 0: his upper arms are abducted to about shoulder height and his elbows are extended, so his arms form a T with the palms up. Frame 1: his upper arms stay in the same abducted position while both elbows flex, bringing the handles beside his head in a double-biceps pose. Only the forearms move between the frames. The shoulders, torso and stance stay still, and nothing presses, pulls down or rows. That is the high cable curl: a standing, two-arm curl between two high pulleys with the upper arms held parallel to the floor and the hands curled toward the ears. The withdrawn High_Cable_Curls photo is mislabelled in the source; I viewed it and it shows a lying-on-bench extension. This photo shows the standing two-pulley curl the audit said was missing. The equipment (cable), laterality (both arms at once), body position (standing) and movement (elbow flexion) all match.
